concepts.title: Framing an A/B test
concepts.outcome: State the change being tested, the effect it should have, and the metrics that will show whether it did.

keyPoints.text: An A/B test begins with a clear hypothesis about what the change should do. Split a complex change into simpler ones, each with its own hypothesis, so the impact of each part can be measured.
keyPoints.locator: Formulate your Hypothesis and Success Metrics

keyPoints.text: The hypothesis should name the metrics that will judge it, so the test can show it to be wrong. A claim such as 'this improves the brand' cannot be tested without a metric that measures brand.
keyPoints.locator: Formulate your Hypothesis and Success Metrics

keyPoints.text: Comparing with a randomised control group cancels biases that affect both groups alike. Each group's own numbers may be off, but the difference between treatment and control can still be right.
keyPoints.locator: 4.1 Clinical Biases, Selection Bias and Fig 4.1

anchor.end: magnitude as that in the population

concepts.title: Random assignment
concepts.outcome: Explain why units are assigned to variants at random, and what randomisation does and does not guarantee.

keyPoints.text: Assigning variants at random means no one, knowingly or not, can steer units with better prospects into one group. That removes a bias known to have a strong effect on outcomes.

anchor.end: very strong effect on outcome variables

keyPoints.text: Randomisation also tends to balance the groups on other factors that affect the outcome, including ones nobody knows about, so those factors are not confused with the effect of the treatment.

anchor.end: with respect to the prognostic variables

keyPoints.text: Preventing imbalance by randomising beats adjusting for it afterwards. An adjustment model can only correct for factors someone knew about, and its assumptions may be wrong.
Letting someone choose each assignment invites large biases, and even a fixed pattern such as alternating can be discovered, which can also lead to bias. Random allocation is preferred.

misconceptions.claim: Random assignment guarantees that the two groups are identical.
misconceptions.correction: Simple randomisation can leave the groups unequal in size, or unbalanced in factors that affect the outcome, especially when samples are small.

concepts.title: The unit of randomisation
concepts.outcome: Choose what to randomise (a cookie, a user, a cluster or an organisation) and recognise when that choice biases the result.

keyPoints.text: Cookie-based IDs are easy to use but unstable: a user who clears cookies can land in the other variant on the next visit. They suit short tests, not estimates of long-term effects.
keyPoints.locator: Choose the Appropriate Unit of Randomization, Stability of the Id

keyPoints.text: If one user's treatment changes what their contacts experience, each user's outcome no longer depends only on their own assignment. Randomising whole clusters of connected users is a common remedy.
keyPoints.locator: Choose the Appropriate Unit of Randomization, Network Effects

keyPoints.text: Business constraints can force a coarser unit. If a feature must reach a whole organisation to work, its users cannot be randomised one by one.
keyPoints.locator: Choose the Appropriate Unit of Randomization, Enterprise Constraints

concepts.title: Choosing metrics
concepts.outcome: Pick metrics that answer the experiment's question, measure them without bias, and know when a proxy metric can mislead.

keyPoints.text: What you measure must match what the experiment is meant to find out, and the way it is measured must be accurate.

Compute a standard core of metrics on every experiment in a product, covering user satisfaction, guardrails, feature engagement and data quality, so that regressions in important metrics are caught whatever feature is being tested.
keyPoints.locator: Formulate your Hypothesis and Success Metrics

anchor.end: which feature we are testing on

keyPoints.text: Changes often improve one thing while quietly hurting another. A broad metric set that covers most of the product is what lets a ship decision weigh the gains against the losses.
keyPoints.locator: Capture Unexpected Effects Early with a Complete Metric Set

keyPoints.text: A proxy metric stands in for the outcome you really care about when that outcome is too slow or costly to measure. It is only useful if it is strongly tied to that outcome.

concepts.title: Overall evaluation criterion and guardrail metrics
concepts.outcome: Tell the metric a test is trying to move from the metrics it must not harm, and decide what to do when they disagree.

keyPoints.text: The overall evaluation criterion (OEC) captures the product's overall goal, usually user satisfaction or loyalty. Guardrail metrics, like page load time or crash rate, track what must not get worse, though the test is not trying to improve it.
The decision is easy when the metrics tell one story: the OEC rises (or stays flat in a test with enough power) and the guardrails improve, or the reverse.
There is no standard way to weigh tradeoffs between key metrics. One method is to weight the metrics, with weights set in advance rather than for the specific test being analysed.

concepts.title: Null and alternative hypotheses
concepts.outcome: Write the null and alternative hypotheses for an A/B comparison, and choose a one- or two-sided test from the question being asked.

keyPoints.text: The null hypothesis says there is no difference in the population; the alternative hypothesis says there is some difference.

anchor.start: The statement that there is not
anchor.end: statement that there is some difference

keyPoints.text: Hypotheses are statements about the population, not the sample. For a difference between two groups the null value is usually 0, and the null hypothesis always contains the equality.
The research question sets the direction. 'Is B different from A?' calls for a two-sided test; 'is B better than A?' calls for a one-sided test.

concepts.title: The p-value
concepts.outcome: Say what a p-value measures in an A/B test, and what it does not.

keyPoints.text: The p-value answers one question: if there were truly no difference, how often would chance alone give a result at least as extreme as the one observed?

anchor.start: we will compute the probability that

keyPoints.text: A result is statistically significant when its p-value is at or below the significance level, alpha. The most common choice of alpha is 0.05.

anchor.start: A test is considered to be

keyPoints.text: A significant result means the difference seen is unlikely to be just random sampling variation.

anchor.end: unlikely due to random sampling variation

misconceptions.claim: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 97% chance that B is better than A.
misconceptions.correction: The p-value is calculated assuming A and B are the same, and says how often chance alone would produce a gap this large. Dashboards that show its complement as a 'chance of beating the original' are relabelling it, not computing that chance.

misconceptions.claim: The p-value is the probability that the result is due to chance alone.
misconceptions.correction: A p-value does not measure the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone, nor the probability that the hypothesis studied is true.

concepts.title: Type I and Type II errors
concepts.outcome: Name the two ways a test's decision can be wrong, say what each costs in an A/B test, and explain how alpha and beta trade off.

keyPoints.text: A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is really true: in an A/B test, declaring a difference that does not exist, produced only by random sampling variation.
keyPoints.locator: 6.1 Type I and Type II Errors

anchor.end: known as a Type I error

keyPoints.text: A Type II error is failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is false: missing a difference that really exists.
keyPoints.locator: 6.1 Type I and Type II Errors

anchor.end: we made a Type II error

keyPoints.text: Alpha is chosen before any data are collected, after weighing what each type of error would cost in the situation at hand.

anchor.start: As we saw in the examples

keyPoints.text: Where a false positive would do more harm than a false negative, a smaller alpha is used. That makes the null harder to reject but lowers the chance of a Type I error.
For a fixed sample size, lowering alpha raises beta, the chance of a Type II error. Lowering both at once needs a larger sample.

anchor.start: If the sample size is fixed
anchor.end: we should increase the sample size

concepts.title: Statistical versus practical significance
concepts.outcome: Judge whether a statistically significant A/B result is large enough to matter, and explain why large tests make tiny effects significant.

keyPoints.text: Practical significance is about the size of the difference, the effect size, and whether it is big enough to matter in real life. What counts as meaningful depends on the context.

Statistical significance depends heavily on sample size: with a very large sample, even tiny differences become significant. The effect size does not grow with the sample, so check it whenever a result is significant.

anchor.end: not directly influenced by sample size

keyPoints.text: A true difference is rarely exactly zero, so a large enough sample can reject almost any null hypothesis. That is why statistical and practical significance must be judged separately.

anchor.end: between statistical significance and practical significance

misconceptions.claim: A statistically significant result means the change had a large or important effect.
misconceptions.correction: A p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.

concepts.title: Tests for two independent groups
concepts.outcome: Choose a test for comparing a rate or a mean between two independent groups, and check that its conditions hold.

keyPoints.text: To compare a rate such as conversion between two groups: with at least 10 successes and 10 failures in each group, the difference between the two sample proportions is approximately normal, so the normal approximation can be used.
When the normal approximation's assumption is met, that method is typically preferred; when it is not, Fisher's exact method, bootstrapping or randomisation methods can be used.

anchor.start: if the assumption above is met

keyPoints.text: These tests assume the two groups are independent: no unit appears in both groups, and the groups are not paired.

To compare means, such as revenue per user, the t distribution can be used when both groups have at least 30 units or the populations are roughly normal. Otherwise, use bootstrapping or a randomisation test.

anchor.end: bootstrapping or randomization) may be used

keyPoints.text: A randomisation test resamples the data to build the distribution a statistic would have if the null hypothesis were true, so that distribution is centred on the null value.

concepts.title: Confidence interval for a difference
concepts.outcome: Build and read a confidence interval for the difference between two variants, and connect it to the test result.

keyPoints.text: A confidence interval is centred on the point estimate (in an A/B test, the observed difference between variants) and reaches out by the margin of error on each side. The margin of error is half the interval's width.

anchor.start: At the center of a confidence

keyPoints.text: For conversion rates, the interval is the difference between the two sample proportions, plus or minus a multiplier times the standard error of that difference.
If a 95% interval for the difference does not contain 0, a difference of zero is not plausible, and you can conclude the two groups differ.

anchor.start: This confidence interval does not contain
anchor.end: conclude that there is a difference

keyPoints.text: Intervals and two-sided tests usually agree. If the 95% interval contains the null value, a test at alpha 0.05 will almost always fail to reject; if it excludes that value, the test will almost always reject.

anchor.end: almost always reject the null hypothesis

keyPoints.text: With the same sample proportion, a sample of 200 gave a narrower confidence interval than a sample of 20.
keyPoints.locator: 4.6 Impact of Sample Size on Confidence Intervals

concepts.title: Statistical power
concepts.outcome: Explain what power is, what raises it, and why an underpowered test that finds nothing proves little.

keyPoints.text: Power is the probability that a test rejects the null hypothesis when the null is false: the chance of detecting a difference that really exists. It equals one minus beta.

anchor.end: of committing a type II error

keyPoints.text: Power goes up with a larger sample, a smaller standard error, a bigger true difference or a higher alpha. A one-sided test also has more power than a two-sided one.

anchor.start: The power of a test can

keyPoints.text: Failing to reject the null does not show the null is true. Either there really is no difference, or the sample was too small to detect the one that exists.

anchor.start: When the null hypothesis cannot be

misconceptions.claim: A test that found no significant difference shows the change has no effect.
misconceptions.correction: A test only guards against Type I error, so it can show evidence against the null but not support for it. A non-significant result may mean no effect, or a sample too small to detect one.

anchor.start: When we perform a hypothesis test
anchor.end: is not large enough to reject

concepts.title: Planning the sample size
concepts.outcome: Name the inputs a sample size calculation needs, and explain how the smallest effect worth detecting drives the number.

keyPoints.text: The sample size for a test is set by the significance level, the power wanted (commonly 80% or 90%) and the smallest effect worth detecting.
The sample needed grows with the square of the noise relative to the effect. Halving the smallest effect you want to detect roughly quadruples the sample.

anchor.start: Notice that the sample size expression

keyPoints.text: Sample size calculations are approximations built on assumed inputs, such as how variable the outcome is, and those assumptions may not hold exactly.
Splitting traffic equally between the variants gives the most power, provided the outcome is equally variable in both.
Power sets a floor on how many units must actually experience the change. If only a small share of traffic is affected, the test needs enough total traffic for that share to reach the floor.
keyPoints.locator: Formulate your Hypothesis and Success Metrics

concepts.title: Peeking and early stopping
concepts.outcome: Explain why stopping a test when it first looks significant inflates false positives, and name the designs that allow valid early looks.

keyPoints.text: The usual significance calculation assumes the sample size was fixed in advance. Running a test until a significant difference appears breaks that assumption, and the reported significance levels lose their meaning.
Testing data again and again as it accumulates raises the Type I error rate, so methods for interim looks aim to keep that rate under control.

anchor.end: controlling the type I error rate

keyPoints.text: The inflation can be large. In a worked example capped at 150 observations, checking after every one and stopping at the first 5% significant result gave false positives about 26% of the time.
keyPoints.locator: How big of a problem is this?

keyPoints.text: A group sequential design stops at an interim look only if the test statistic crosses that look's boundary, and the boundaries are chosen so that the overall significance level stays within the target.
Stopping a test early, for example because of a significant difference, biases the estimate of the effect, and the earlier the stop, the larger the bias.

anchor.end: potential for a lot of bias

misconceptions.claim: It is fine to stop an A/B test as soon as it reaches significance.
misconceptions.correction: Stopping an experiment at a significant-looking result inflates the false-positive rate, and the more often you peek, the further off the significance levels become.
misconceptions.locator: How big of a problem is this?

misconceptions.claim: You should not look at an A/B test at all until it ends.
misconceptions.correction: Measuring throughout a test is essential so problems can be caught, but early results need stronger significance levels, and otherwise the test should run its planned duration.

anchor.start: at ExP, to make early results

concepts.title: Many metrics and multiple comparisons
concepts.outcome: Recognise when many tests are being run at once, estimate how many false positives to expect, and adjust for them.

keyPoints.text: At alpha 0.05, each test has a 5% chance of a false positive when there is no real difference. Run 100 such tests and about 5 will look significant by chance alone.

anchor.start: If we are conducting a hypothesis

keyPoints.text: The Bonferroni correction divides alpha by the number of tests, so three tests at 0.05 are each judged against about 0.0167. It is simple but conservative, which raises the risk of missing real effects.
keyPoints.locator: 6.3 Issues with Multiple Testing, Quick Correction for Multiple Tests

anchor.start: For instance, if you are comparing

keyPoints.text: With two primary outcomes, adjust alpha if the test counts as a success when either one moves. If success needs both to move, no adjustment is needed.
keyPoints.locator: 8.7 Adjustment Factors for Sample Size Calculations

anchor.start: there are two primary outcome variables

keyPoints.text: Running a pairwise comparison over and over, for every pair of variants, does not hold the overall significance level at the level set for one comparison.
keyPoints.locator: 7.4.7, Multiple Comparison test procedures are needed

misconceptions.claim: If any one of our twenty metrics is significant at 0.05, the change had a real effect.
misconceptions.correction: When there is more than one primary outcome or comparison, the significance level should be adjusted so the overall false-positive rate is not inflated.
misconceptions.locator: 8.7 Adjustment Factors for Sample Size Calculations

anchor.start: more than one primary outcome variable

misconceptions.claim: If the overall result is flat, slicing it by segment until one shows a significant lift reveals who the change works for.
misconceptions.correction: Comparisons chosen after seeing the results do not carry the confidence level the procedure states. Decide the comparisons in advance, or use a procedure built for comparisons chosen after the data are in.
misconceptions.locator: 7.4.7, Determine contrasts in advance of observing the experimental results

anchor.end: use after observing the experimental results

concepts.title: Segments and effects that change over time
concepts.outcome: Break results down by segment and by day without fooling yourself, and recognise a novelty effect.

keyPoints.text: A change can affect different users differently, so results are often broken down by segments such as market, browser or app version to find where the effect differs.
keyPoints.locator: Slice the Analysis with the Appropriate Segments

keyPoints.text: Segment sizes must stay balanced between treatment and control. Segments whose membership is fixed independently of the treatment stay balanced whenever the overall test does.
keyPoints.locator: Use Segments that are Stable during the A/B Test

keyPoints.text: Break results down by day. An effect that shrinks quickly from day to day suggests a novelty effect; a spike on a single day suggests a data problem or a one-off event.
Reading results early in a test can bias a team toward changes that give only a temporary improvement.

anchor.end: a temporary improvement to the product

concepts.title: Sample ratio mismatch and data quality
concepts.outcome: Check that a test's traffic split and data are sound before reading its results.

keyPoints.text: A sample ratio mismatch (SRM) is when the split of users between treatment and control differs from the split the test was set up with. An SRM usually invalidates the test.
keyPoints.locator: Set Up Alerts to Detect Unintended Degradations

keyPoints.text: Test for SRM early and alert on it, so a broken test can be investigated, and stopped if it cannot be saved.
keyPoints.locator: Set Up Alerts to Detect Unintended Degradations

anchor.end: if the results are not salvageable

keyPoints.text: SRM is the earliest validity check, but passing it overall does not rule out an imbalance within an individual metric.
keyPoints.locator: Check for Imbalance in Metric Observation Units

keyPoints.text: A ratio metric such as clicks per session can move only because its denominator moved. The denominator is a metric in its own right; if it shifts significantly, the ratio can move unexpectedly.
keyPoints.locator: Check for Imbalance in Metric Observation Units

anchor.end: unexpected movements in the rate metric

keyPoints.text: Before reading results, confirm that the user count in each variant matches the planned allocation, and that metrics the change should obviously move did move.
keyPoints.locator: Ensure Metric Movements Align with the Test Set-Up

concepts.title: Sanity-checking surprising results
concepts.outcome: Treat a surprising result with suspicion, check for bias that was there before the test, and know when to re-run.

keyPoints.text: Twyman's law suggests that a very large effect from a feature that few users engage with may not be trustworthy.

anchor.end: a large effect on user satisfaction

keyPoints.text: The strongest check on a treatment effect is reproducing it: re-run the test on a fresh sample of users and see whether a comparable effect appears.

Comparing the two groups on the same metric before the test began (a retrospective A/A check) shows whether the randomisation itself produced a gap. A gap there makes a borderline result in the test suspect.
keyPoints.locator: Check and Account for Pre-Experiment Bias, Retrospective-AA Analysis

prerequisites.reason: The null and alternative hypotheses formalise the product hypothesis.
Choosing what to randomise presumes knowing why randomisation matters.
A sample ratio mismatch is a departure from the planned random split.
The OEC and guardrails are kinds of metric with different jobs.
A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true.
Each two-group test checks a null hypothesis of no difference.
Both errors are wrong decisions made by comparing a p-value with alpha.
Statistical significance is defined through the p-value.
Power is one minus the Type II error rate.
A sample size is chosen to reach a target power.
The smallest effect worth detecting is a practical-significance judgement.
Peeking is a problem because it inflates the Type I error rate.
The plain remedy for peeking is to fix the sample size in advance.
Multiple testing inflates the overall Type I error rate.
Each segment read is one more comparison.
